payload.name: waveform-coding
payload.scope: So a continuous signal can be carried and stored at a fixed reduced bit rate with its waveform shape preserved, in contrast to parametric coding, which transmits only a model of the source.

definition.body: Waveform-coding is a human-made family of signal-coding procedures that encode the signal's own waveform - the sequence of sample amplitudes - rather than a model of the source, so a continuous signal can be carried or stored at a fixed reduced bit rate with the waveform shape preserved. The family's procedures act on the waveform itself: pulse-code modulation quantizes the sample values directly; delta modulation encodes the difference between successive samples; adaptive differential pulse-code modulation quantizes the prediction error against an adaptive predictor; sigma-delta modulation emits an oversampled one-bit feedback stream. Parameters that define the class: (1) the bit commitment to the waveform, fixed or adaptive; (2) the representation of each sample - direct amplitude level, successive difference, or prediction error; (3) the reconstruction rule that maps the code word back to a sample. Persistence mechanism: specified in the ITU-T G.711, G.721, G.726 standards and the CD Red Book, described in the speech-coding literature as the waveform-coding class alongside parametric and hybrid coding, and implemented in telephony, music disc, and audio-coding practice. e.g.: the G.711 mu-law PCM codec in a T1 voice path; the G.726 24 kbit/s ADPCM codec in an ISDN voice channel; the 16-bit linear PCM of a Red Book CD track | not: linear predictive coding which transmits a model of the vocal tract rather than the waveform; the code-excited linear prediction of G.729 which synthesizes speech from codebook excitation through a synthesis filter; transform coding of a coefficient vector in the frequency domain [formal: codificatio formae undae | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: delta-modulation
payload.scope: So that a continuous signal can be carried at one bit per sample, below the rate where a multi-bit quantizer is worth its complexity, with a one-sample prediction stage preserving most of the waveform.

definition.body: Delta modulation is a human-made one-bit predictive waveform-coding procedure that transmits, for each new sample, only the sign of the difference between the sample and the previously reconstructed value, so a continuous signal can be carried on one bit per sample. Procedure: (1) a predictor holds the last reconstructed sample; (2) the encoder compares the new sample with it and transmits one bit, up or down; (3) the decoder reconstructs the sample as the previous sample plus or minus a step, fixed in basic delta modulation and adapted to the signal slope in adaptive delta modulation. Parameters: (1) the bit commitment, one bit per sample; (2) the step size, fixed or adaptive; (3) the predictor order, the previous sample in first-order delta modulation, a linear combination in differential forms; (4) the sampling rate, at the Nyquist rate in classic delta modulation, where oversampled one-bit variants with noise-shaped feedback are sigma-delta modulation instead. Persistence mechanism: proposed by Zeller in 1948 for long-distance telephone lines, realized in Bell System first-order delta-modulation voice experiments at 256 kbit/s, carried in the differential lineage of the ITU-T G.721 and G.726 standards, and described in the coding literature as the one-bit ancestor of differential pulse-code modulation. e.g.: Zeller's 1948 delta modulation proposal for long-distance telephone lines; first-order delta modulation voice channel at 256 kbit/s in Bell System experiments; one-bit delta modulation telemetry channel in a satellite downlink | not: sigma-delta modulation (oversampled one-bit noise-shaped feedback stream); pulse-code modulation (multi-bit quantizer on the full sample, no prediction stage); adaptive differential pulse-code modulation (multi-bit prediction-error quantizer, G.726) [formal: modulatio deltae | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: log-law-quantizer
payload.scope: So that speech and audio signals can be quantized at low bit rates while keeping quantization noise perceptually uniform across the signal's dynamic range.

definition.body: A log-law quantizer is a human-made quantization structure whose step sizes scale logarithmically with signal amplitude, so that small amplitudes receive fine steps and large amplitudes receive coarse steps, achieving a near-constant signal-to-quantization-noise ratio across the input dynamic range. Procedure: the quantizer maps input amplitudes to quantization levels using a piecewise-logarithmic step-size function — at each amplitude level a, the step size Δ(a) = Δ₀ · r^(⌊a⌋) for base rate Δ₀ and growth ratio r > 1, producing a nonuniform partition of the amplitude range that preserves perceptual fidelity. Parameters: (1) the step-size growth ratio r, typically 1.5–2.0 per step; (2) the number of quantization levels, commonly 64 in predictive codecs; (3) the dynamic range covered, the ratio between maximum and minimum step sizes. Persistence mechanism: implemented as a lookup table in telephony and audio codec hardware, specified in ITU-T standards (G.726 ADPCM uses a 64-entry table), described in speech-coding textbooks as the canonical nonuniform quantizer, and deployed in conference-bridge and ISDN voice codecs. e.g.: the 64-entry log-law quantizer in ITU-T G.726 ADPCM codec; the μ-law 8-bit quantizer in North American T1 telephony; the A-law 8-bit quantizer in European E1 telephony | not: linear PCM quantizer, which uses uniform step sizes; companding, which uses a preprocessing nonlinearity with uniform quantization [formal: quantizatio logarithmica | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: mu-law
payload.scope: So that a wide dynamic range speech signal can be carried in 8 bits per sample on digital telephony while keeping small signals quiet.

definition.body: A mu-law nonlinearity is a human-made piecewise-logarithmic companding compressor curve that fits a wide dynamic range signal into a small number of uniform quantization steps. Procedure: (1) compress the input amplitude through the mu-law curve mu(x) = sign(x)·ln(1+mu·|x|)/ln(1+mu), (2) apply a uniform 8-bit quantizer to the compressed value, (3) at the receiver expand through the inverse curve to reconstruct a linear output. Parameters: (1) the compression constant mu, 255 in North American T1 practice; (2) the number of quantization bits, 8; (3) the sample rate, 8 kHz for telephony speech. Persistence mechanism: standardized in ITU-T G.711 (1972) and deployed in T1 (DS1) digital voice channels and G.711 mu-law codecs in gateways and IP telephony hardware, described in DSP and telephony textbooks, and implemented in every telephony codec path that carries a 64 kbit/s speech channel. e.g.: the mu-law 8-bit 3.1 kHz telephone channel of ITU-T G.711 on T1 lines; the g711u mu-law sample in an Asterisk SIP voice channel; the mu-law 8-bit sample in an ISDN basic rate interface bearer channel | not: A-law (the E1 log-law curve with a different formula and no mu parameter); linear 8-bit PCM (uniform steps across the full range, no compression); a dynamic-range compressor for audio mixing (loudness shaping, not a quantizer nonlinearity) [formal: compressio mu | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cepstral-mean-subtraction
payload.scope: So that cepstral feature vectors are centered and normalized for robust spectral shape comparison across sessions.

definition.body: Cepstral-mean-subtraction is a human-made normalization procedure that centers cepstral coefficient vectors by subtracting their frame-wise or session-wise mean, removing static offset to emphasize spectral shape over absolute level. Procedure: (1) compute the mean of each cepstral coefficient dimension over a sliding window (typically 301-501 ms) or an entire utterance/session, (2) subtract that mean from each cepstral coefficient value, (3) output the zero-mean cepstral coefficients. Parameters: (1) the window length for mean computation, (2) the cepstral coefficient dimensions included, (3) whether to apply per-frame or global mean. Persistence mechanism: implemented in speech recognition frontends such as Kaldi's cmvn and apply-cmvn tools, HTK's cepstral mean normalization, and standard feature normalization pipelines in speaker recognition systems. e.g.: Kaldi's cmvn tool applied to MFCC features in the LibriSpeech speech recognition pipeline; HTK cepstral mean normalization applied to Aurora-4 evaluation features; the apply-cmvn step in a Kaldi i-vector speaker recognition frontend | not: cepstral-mean (the scalar value itself, not the normalization procedure); cepstral-variance-normalization (divides by standard deviation in addition to subtracting mean, not just mean removal) [formal: subtractio medi cepstralis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cepstral-peak-to-average-ratio
payload.scope: So that the prominence of periodic structure in the cepstrum can be measured as a single scalar for pitch and voicing detection.

definition.body: Cepstral-peak-to-average-ratio is a human-made scalar feature computed from cepstral coefficients that measures the prominence of the dominant periodic component relative to the overall cepstral energy. Procedure: (1) compute the cepstrum of a signal frame, (2) identify the maximum-magnitude cepstral coefficient within a quefrency range of interest (typically corresponding to the expected pitch period), (3) compute the arithmetic mean of all cepstral coefficients in that range, (4) divide the peak value by the mean to obtain the ratio. Parameters: (1) the quefrency range for peak detection, (2) whether to use absolute magnitude or signed value, (3) the number of cepstral coefficients included. Persistence mechanism: used in pitch detection and voicing decision systems, described in speech processing literature for periodicity measurement, and implemented in research speech analysis toolkits. e.g.: peak-to-average cepstral ratio in a pitch detection algorithm for the Aurora-4 speech recognition evaluation; cepstral peak prominence measurement in Kaldi's pitch estimation tools; the cepstral peak-to-mean ratio in the CMU Sphinx voicing decision pipeline | not: cepstrum-energy (sum of squared coefficients, not peak-to-average ratio); cepstral-peak-picking (identifies peak locations, not the ratio of peak to mean) [formal: ratio acmen-medii cepstralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes]

[5 carving] The definition's formula is not self-consistent, which item 5 requires ('formulas consistent with themselves'). The filed curve is 'piecewise-linear with slope 1 near the origin and logarithmic above |x| = 1/A'. Arithmetic: with the log branch in its standard normalized form f(x)=(1+ln(1+A|x|))/(1+ln A) and A=87.6, the breakpoint 1/A = 0.0114 gives log-branch value 0.309, but a slope-1 linear branch reaches only 0.0114 there — a 27x discontinuity at the curve's own join. No curve that jumps at its breakpoint is a defined characteristic. The real ITU-T G.711 a-law (A=87.6) is the smooth logarithmic characteristic (1+ln(1+A|x|))/(1+ln A) (or its standard piecewise form with the linear segment's slope and breakpoint set to the continuity values, slope (1+ln A)/(1+A) at the join 1/(1+ln A) = 0.183, not slope 1 at 1/A). The filed description matches neither: the stated slope (1) and the stated breakpoint (1/A) cannot coexist with any continuous a-law. Item 5 fails; the rest of the filing (scope, referent, name, trailer, examples) is sound, so a corrected re-filing or a corrected definition would stand — but this one does not.

payload.name: cepstrum-interpolation
payload.scope: A human-made signal processing procedure that computes intermediate cepstral vectors between two or more existing cepstral frames, producing smooth transitions in the quefrency domain for time-varying speech manipulation.

definition.body: Cepstrum-interpolation is a signal processing procedure that generates intermediate cepstral coefficient vectors between two or more existing frames by computing a weighted combination in the quefrency domain. Procedure: (1) given source cepstral frames c[1] and c[2] at different time points, (2) compute an interpolation factor alpha in [0,1] based on the desired time position, (3) calculate c_interp = (1-alpha)*c[1] + alpha*c[2] element-wise on the cepstral coefficients, optionally adding back the mean-removed components. Parameters: (1) the cepstral frames to interpolate, (2) the interpolation factor or time schedule, (3) the coefficient dimensions included (typically the full vector or a subset). Persistence mechanism: implemented in speech synthesis systems (e.g., HTS hidden Markov model-based synthesis, World vocoder for voice conversion), voice conversion pipelines, and formant-preserving time-stretching algorithms. e.g.: HTS (Hidden Markov Model-based Speech) system for interpolating cepstral vectors between HMM states during synthesis; World vocoder cepstral interpolation for natural voice conversion with smooth formant transitions; STRAIGHT vocoder cepstral interpolation in prosody-preserving speech editing; Kaldi's TTS frontend cepstral interpolation between acoustic model frames | not: cepstrum-decomposition (separates source and filter, not interpolates between frames); cepstrum-smoothing (applies a window function to reduce noise rather than interpolating between frames) [formal: interpolatio cepstrorum | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cepstral-acceleration
payload.scope: A human-made speech processing feature that computes the second-order temporal derivative of cepstral coefficient trajectories, capturing the rate of change of the spectral envelope's velocity over time.

definition.body: Cepstral-acceleration (also called delta-delta or double-delta) is a speech processing feature that computes the second-order temporal derivative of cepstral coefficient trajectories, capturing how the rate of spectral envelope change itself varies over time. Procedure: (1) compute the first-order delta features for each cepstral coefficient dimension using least-squares regression over a window of frames; (2) apply the same regression procedure to the delta features to obtain the acceleration (second derivative) for each coefficient; alternatively, compute a single regression over a wider window and take the quadratic coefficient. Parameters: (1) the input cepstral coefficient frames, (2) the regression window size (typically 5-7 frames, wider than for delta), (3) the frame shift (standard 10 ms). Acceleration features complement static and delta features in speech recognition by encoding curvature of spectral trajectories. Persistence: implemented in Kaldi's compute-kaldi-deltas (which computes delta-delta), HTK's acceleration feature extraction, and standard HMM-based speech recognition pipelines. e.g.: Kaldi's compute-kaldi-deltas tool computing delta-delta from MFCC features; HTK acceleration features in Aurora-4 speech recognition evaluation; CMU Sphinx delta-delta features for dynamic model training; the acceleration component in NIST speech recognition feature extraction baseline | not: cepstral-delta (first-order derivative per coefficient, not second-order); cepstral-rate (aggregate L2-norm of first difference, not per-coefficient second derivative) [formal: acceleratio-cestralis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

[3 test] the note argues that removing the log-law quantizer stops ADPCM from operating. But ADPCM is the broader adaptive predictive codec framework; the log-law quantizer is one implementation choice within that framework. ITU-T G.726 specifies a 64-entry log-law quantizer, but ADPCM as a concept does not require log-law — it could use linear quantization or other non-uniform schemes. The accepted ADPCM definition describes what G.726 does, not what makes ADPCM ADPCM. Removing the log-law quantizer does not stop the adaptive differential prediction-coding concept from operating; it just changes the quantization law used.

payload.name: cross-cepstrum
payload.scope: People made the cross-cepstrum to estimate the time delay between two signals robustly, in the quefrency domain, when the two signals' spectra differ or the environment is noisy.

definition.body: The cross-cepstrum is a signal-processing transform that measures the time delay between two signals in the quefrency domain. Procedure: (1) compute the FFTs X(f) and Y(f) of the two signals x(t) and y(t); (2) form the cross-spectrum X(f) times the complex conjugate of Y(f); (3) take the inverse FFT to obtain the cross-cepstrum c(tau); (4) the peak of c(tau) at quefrency tau-hat is the time offset between the signals. Unlike the single-signal cepstrum, the cross-cepstrum applies no logarithm: the log separates spectral envelope from fine structure in one signal, while for delay estimation the conjugate product of the two spectra suffices, and the conjugate symmetry of the cross-spectrum keeps the result real. Parameters: (1) the two signals whose inter-signal delay is to be estimated; (2) the FFT length and window applied to each signal; (3) the quefrency search range or peak-selection window around the expected delay. Persistence mechanism: introduced by Flate (1979) for the identification of delayed echoes in noisy speech; maintained in the DSP literature and in signal toolkits as a robust time-delay estimator, used in microphone-pair delay estimation, echo identification, and cross-signal alignment where the two spectra differ. e.g.: cross-cepstrum echo-delay identification in noisy speech (Flate, IEEE Trans. ASSP 1979); cross-cepstrum time-delay estimation between a microphone pair for source localization in a reverberant room | not: the cepstrum, cross-correlation [formal: cepstrum transversum | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

definition.body: The complex cepstrum is a signal-processing representation computed by taking the inverse Fourier transform of the complex logarithm of a signal's full complex spectrum. Unlike the real cepstrum which uses the log of the power spectrum, the complex cepstrum preserves phase information from the original spectrum, enabling phase reconstruction and minimum-phase/max-phase decomposition. Procedure: (1) compute the FFT to obtain the complex spectrum X(f); (2) compute the natural logarithm of each complex spectral value, yielding ln|X(f)| + j·arg(X(f)); (3) apply the inverse FFT to obtain the complex cepstrum sequence. Parameters: (1) the input signal, (2) FFT length, (3) handling of spectral zeros (adding epsilon before log). Persistence: documented in Oppenheim and Schafer Digital Signal Processing, used in minimum-phase signal reconstruction, homomorphic deconvolution with phase, and speech analysis where phase reconstruction is required. e.g.: minimum-phase reconstruction from magnitude spectrum via complex cepstrum (Oppenheim and Schafer DSP); complex cepstrum homomorphic deconvolution in seismic signal processing | not: real-cepstrum (uses log of power spectrum magnitude, discards phase); cepstrum (general term that may refer to either variant) [formal: cepstrum complexum | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]
